datasets: 311 Customer Service Requests (current year) - Open Baltimore ArcGIS FeatureServer, newest 20,000 with neighborhood, fetched at runtime
Vacant Building Notices (Open) - DHCD Open Baltimore ArcGIS FeatureServer, all ~11,481 rows, fetched at runtime
concurrency_primitives: goroutine per dataset + buffered result channels + select + context cancel (ingest/ingest.go:13-50); bounded semaphore channel (runtime.NumCPU()) worker pool over 2000-record chunks producing private partial aggregates sent on a channel to a single merging goroutine, WaitGroup + closer goroutine (processor/processor.go:78-115); one goroutine per question writing its own slot + WaitGroup (analytics/analytics.go:25-39); signal.NotifyContext + WithTimeout (main.go:30-33)
design_patterns: Pipeline (ingest -> processor -> analytics -> ui as separate packages passing plain structs), generic Template/Strategy paged ArcGIS client fetchLayer[T], fan-out/fan-in worker pool with semaphore and single-owner merge, higher-order RunAll over question functions, generic Result abstraction for rendering
questions: Q1 Top 5 neighborhoods by combined vacant notices + 311 requests
Q2 Pearson correlation of vacancy counts with 311 request categories across neighborhoods
Q3 Open vs closed 311 share in top-quartile-vacancy neighborhoods vs all others
Q4 Top 3 ZIP codes by open code-enforcement 311 requests + vacant notices
Q5 Data density (total/mean/median/max per neighborhood) for 311, open 311 and vacancies
stakeholders: generic 'municipal stakeholders' - no office explicitly named
overview: Idiomatic four-package Go pipeline (ingest/processor/analytics/ui) with a thin main orchestrator, Go generics for a paged ArcGIS client, a generic Result type rendered by a reusable table/histogram package, deterministic sorting, and context-based cancellation throughout. Code is gofmt/vet clean, well commented, and the detailed README matches it exactly; the only maintainability gap is the lack of unit tests for the pure join and statistics functions.
stakeholder_value: Real value: the Pearson analysis shows sanitation/dumping 311 requests track vacancy counts (r=+0.70) far more than transportation requests (r=+0.26), which tells DHCD/DPW where to co-target cleanup with abatement; the ZIP ranking (21217, 21223, 21213) is directly actionable for code enforcement; and the open-rate comparison shows high-vacancy areas are not being closed out more slowly. Q5 is merely descriptive and stakeholders are implied rather than named.
issues: No data bundled; every run requires live network access to Baltimore ArcGIS endpoints, with no offline or cached fallback
go.mod requires go 1.27.2; built on the Go 1.24 host only because GOTOOLCHAIN=auto downloaded the 1.27.2 toolchain over the network
Only one test and it is a live network integration test; no unit tests for pearson/IsClosed/Category/merge/finalize
Stakeholders not explicitly named; Q5 is single-dataset descriptive statistics
311 side limited to the newest 20,000 records (~2% of the layer), so counts are recency-biased (disclosed)
Vacancies attributed to ZIP via each neighborhood's dominant 311 ZIP, a heuristic that can misallocate
Q4 histogram bar labels show rank numbers instead of ZIP codes
rationale: Full marks for concurrency, run, and README: a correct parallel fetch, bounded mutex-free worker-pool join, parallel analytics, race-clean, running end-to-end in 20 s with sensible real-world answers. Real-data is capped at 10 by the rubric because nothing is bundled (runtime fetch only), build loses one point for depending on an automatic Go 1.27.2 toolchain download, architecture loses one for no unit tests, and stakeholder loses two for implied-not-named stakeholders and a descriptive Q5. Total 90/100, A.
